profile.impact_source: Senior DevOps Engineer, Pulse Data Labs (client: URUS), Feb 2026 – Sep 2026
about: I build delivery platforms that teams can trust: one pipeline that tests, scans, promotes and rolls back on its own, running on infrastructure defined in code.
On the reliability side I define SLOs with application teams, alert on error-budget burn instead of noise, and write postmortems that lead to fixes.
This site collects six hands-on Azure labs I built to show that work end to end. They use synthetic apps, data and incidents, so every lab can be run and checked by anyone.

projects.title: AKS Delivery Platform with Azure DevOps
projects.short: Multi-stage Azure Pipelines that test, build in ACR and promote one image through Dev, QA and Production on AKS, with approvals and automatic rollback.
projects.problem: Releases were copied between environments by hand, Production had no approval gate, and a broken release stayed live until someone noticed. Liveness probes kept passing while the API returned errors.
built: Flask Orders API with health, readiness and version endpoints, plus a switch that simulates a bad release.
Helm chart with rolling updates, PDB, HPA, non-root security context and per-environment values.
Reusable build and deploy templates; the same image tag is promoted Dev → QA → Prod.
Deploy script that records the Helm revision, runs a functional smoke test and runs helm rollback on failure.
Production gated by an approval check on the Azure DevOps environment.
projects.result: Release 1.1.0 failed the smoke test (HTTP 500 on /api/v1/orders). The script rolled back to revision 1 and the restored 1.0.0 passed every check. Verified locally; Azure steps are scripted.

demo.intro: A bad release reaches the cluster. The smoke test catches it and the pipeline rolls back on its own.
captions: Revision 1 deploys orders-api 1.0.0. All four smoke checks pass.
Revision 2 deploys 1.1.0 with a simulated defect. Probes stay green but the orders API returns HTTP 500, so the smoke test fails and the release is rolled back to revision 1.
The release history shows the rollback as revision 3, and /version confirms 1.0.0 is serving again.

lead.built: A multi-stage Azure Pipelines release for a Flask orders API: one image built in ACR, promoted Dev → QA → Prod with Helm on AKS, a Production approval gate, and a deploy script that smoke-tests every release and runs helm rollback when it fails.
verify: Revision 1 deploys orders-api 1.0.0 and all four smoke checks pass.
Revision 2 deploys 1.1.0. Health probes stay green, but the orders API returns HTTP 500, so the smoke test fails.
The script rolls back to revision 1. Helm records it as revision 3, and /version confirms 1.0.0 is serving again.

projects.home_problem: Releases were promoted by hand and a broken release stayed live until someone noticed.
projects.home_result: Release 1.1.0 failed its smoke test; the deploy script rolled back to 1.0.0 automatically.
projects.environment: Azure Pipelines multi-stage YAML, ACR and AKS with three namespaces (orders-dev, orders-qa, orders-prod), deployed with Helm. A Flask orders API stands in for a real service.
scope: Release, smoke test and rollback flow (local Helm stand-in) and 7 unit tests
helm lint and helm template for dev, qa and prod
ACR build, AKS deployment and the Production approval
decisions: Build once, promote the same image tag (the build ID) through Dev, QA and Production, so what was tested is what ships.
Run a functional smoke test after helm upgrade --wait: liveness probes stayed green while the orders API returned HTTP 500.
Record the Helm revision before deploying and roll back to it on failure, then fail the stage so later environments are never touched.
Rolling updates with maxUnavailable 0 and maxSurge 1, a PodDisruptionBudget, and a non-root, read-only container.
projects.failure: Release 1.1.0 contains a simulated defect. Health probes pass, but GET /api/v1/orders and GET /api/v1/orders/ORD-1001 return HTTP 500, so the smoke test fails.
projects.recovery: The script runs helm rollback to revision 1. Helm records the rollback as revision 3, the smoke test passes again against 1.0.0, and the stage is marked failed so QA and Production are not deployed.
projects.evidence_gaps: No run against a real AKS cluster or Azure DevOps organisation is recorded yet; the pipeline, Helm chart and scripts are ready for one.
projects.home_built: Multi-stage Azure Pipelines that build one image in ACR and promote it Dev → QA → Prod on AKS with Helm, an approval gate, smoke tests and automatic rollback.

projects.title: AKS Observability and SRE Incident Lab
projects.short: OpenTelemetry and Prometheus instrumentation, SLOs with error budgets and burn-rate alerts, and a full latency incident from detection to postmortem.
projects.problem: The checkout service had dashboards but no reliability target. Alerts fired on noise, and nobody was paged when checkouts became slow but still returned HTTP 200.
built: checkout-api with OpenTelemetry spans per dependency and a Prometheus latency histogram.
Recording rules for bad-request ratios and multi-window burn-rate alerts (14.4x page, 6x ticket) with a promtool unit test.
Grafana dashboard, OTel Collector, Docker Compose stack and AKS manifests with a PodMonitor for Azure managed Prometheus.
A live incident demo against the real service and a 3-hour minute-by-minute simulation.
Runbook and a blameless postmortem built from the simulation output.
projects.result: Simulated incident: the latency SLO page fired 16 minutes after the fault, span timings pointed to inventory.lookup, the cache fallback mitigated it at T+27 min, and 3.6% of the monthly error budget was used. In the live demo the burn rate went from 0x to over 14.4x and back to 0x.

demo.intro: Checkout gets slow but keeps returning 200. The SLO alert catches it, traces point to the cause, and a fallback restores service.
captions: Baseline: steady traffic, no requests slower than 300 ms, burn rate 0x.
Fault injected in the inventory dependency. More than half of the requests miss the 300 ms objective and the burn rate passes the 14.4x paging threshold.
Slow-request span timings show inventory.lookup taking about 800 ms while payment and persistence stay normal.
The inventory cache fallback is enabled and the burn rate drops back to 0x.
Detected, diagnosed, mitigated and recovered.

lead.built: An instrumented checkout service with OpenTelemetry spans and a Prometheus latency histogram, a 300 ms latency SLO with multi-window burn-rate alerts (14.4x page, 6x ticket), a Grafana dashboard, a runbook and a blameless postmortem.
verify: Alert: a slow inventory dependency pushes the burn rate past the 14.4x paging threshold while checkouts still return HTTP 200.
Investigation: slow-request span timings point to inventory.lookup at about 800 ms; payment and persistence stay normal.
Mitigation: the inventory cache fallback brings the burn rate back to 0x.
Postmortem: in the 3-hour simulation the page fired at 16 minutes, mitigation landed at 27 minutes, 3.6% of the monthly error budget was used, and four action items were recorded.

projects.home_problem: Checkout became slow while still returning HTTP 200, and nobody was paged.
projects.home_result: Simulated incident: the 14.4x burn-rate page fired at 16 minutes, traces pointed to inventory.lookup, and the fallback mitigated at 27 minutes. The live local demo showed the same 0x → 14.4x+ → 0x burn.
projects.environment: checkout-api instrumented with the OpenTelemetry SDK and a Prometheus histogram; Prometheus recording and burn-rate rules, Grafana, and an OTel Collector. The SLO is 99% of POST /api/checkout within 300 ms over 30 days.
scope: Live incident demo against the instrumented service and 8 tests
3-hour minute-by-minute incident timeline used for the postmortem
promtool check rules and promtool test rules
Azure Managed Prometheus, Managed Grafana and Application Insights
decisions: Alert on error-budget burn, not raw latency: a 14.4x page (1-hour and 5-minute windows, for 2 minutes) and a 6x ticket.
Recording rules for bad-request ratios so dashboards and alerts read the same numbers.
One span per dependency, so a slow checkout shows which call is slow without guesswork.
A cache fallback toggle documented in the runbook as the first mitigation.
projects.failure: The inventory dependency slows to about 800 ms. 58% of checkouts miss the 300 ms objective while still returning HTTP 200, and the burn rate passes the 14.4x paging threshold.
projects.recovery: Slow-request span timings point to inventory.lookup. Enabling the inventory cache fallback brings the burn rate back to 0x. The blameless postmortem records 3.6% of the monthly error budget used and four action items.
projects.evidence_gaps: The timeline numbers come from the simulator, not from a production incident. The Azure Monitor setup is documented but has not been run on AKS.
projects.home_built: An OpenTelemetry-instrumented checkout service with a latency SLO, multi-window burn-rate alerts, a runbook and a blameless postmortem.

projects.title: Azure Hub-and-Spoke Infrastructure with Terraform
projects.short: Reusable Terraform modules for hub and spoke VNets, peering, NSGs, private endpoints and private DNS, with remote state and a reproducible DNS incident.
projects.problem: Teams built VNets by hand. Private endpoints were added without matching private DNS links, so workloads silently resolved the public endpoint and failed with HTTP 403.
built: Six modules: hub, spoke, two-way peering, NSG with rule map, private DNS zone with VNet links, private endpoint with DNS zone group.
Lab environment with a storage account that has public access disabled and a private endpoint in the app spoke.
Remote state in Azure Storage with Entra ID auth, versioning and soft delete.
Validation blocks, terraform test files with a mocked provider, and a static checker.
dns_check.py, which explains the resolution path from any VNet using the Terraform dns_model output.
projects.result: With misconfig.tfvars the app spoke resolves storage to a public IP (expected private: FAIL). Linking the zone through Terraform returns the private endpoint 10.1.2.4 (PASS).

demo.intro: A missing private DNS zone link sends traffic to the public endpoint. Terraform fixes it.
captions: Broken state: the app spoke follows the public CNAME and gets a public IP, so the private endpoint is bypassed and storage returns 403.
The data spoke works. Comparing the two shows the privatelink.blob zone is linked to hub and data only.
Terraform adds the missing VNet link. The same lookup from the app spoke now returns the private endpoint IP.
The check expected a private answer and now passes.

projects.home_problem: A private endpoint without a matching private DNS link sent workloads to the public endpoint (HTTP 403).
projects.home_result: The app spoke first resolved a public IP; after Terraform linked the zone it resolved 10.1.2.4.
projects.environment: Terraform with azurerm 4.x: a hub VNet (10.0.0.0/16), app and data spokes (10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16), NSGs, a storage account with public access disabled, a private endpoint and the privatelink.blob private DNS zone. State in Azure Storage with Entra ID auth.
scope: Static checks, 7 tests and the DNS resolution model built from Terraform output
terraform validate and terraform test with a mocked provider
terraform apply and nslookup from a VM in the spoke
decisions: Six small modules (hub, spoke, peering, NSG, private DNS, private endpoint) instead of one large configuration.
Storage public network access disabled and asserted in a terraform test, so private endpoints are the only path.
The DNS zone's VNet links are a map in code, so a missing link shows up in review and in tests.
Remote state with Entra ID auth, versioning and soft delete rather than access keys.
projects.failure: With misconfig.tfvars the privatelink.blob zone is linked to the hub and data VNets only. The app spoke follows the public CNAME, gets public IP 20.60.0.10, and storage rejects the request with HTTP 403.
projects.recovery: Comparing resolution from the data spoke shows the missing link. Applying Terraform without misconfig.tfvars adds the app VNet link, and the same lookup returns the private endpoint 10.1.2.4.
projects.evidence_gaps: DNS answers come from a resolution model driven by Terraform's dns_model output, not from nslookup on Azure.
projects.home_built: Reusable Terraform modules for a hub and two spokes, NSGs, a private endpoint and private DNS links.

projects.title: Azure DevSecOps Software Supply Chain
projects.short: Trivy scanning, SBOM generation and Cosign signing with an Azure Key Vault key, enforced at admission on AKS, with Workload ID for secrets.
projects.problem: Any image that could be pulled could run on AKS. Nobody knew what was inside running images, and workloads used stored credentials to reach secrets.
built: Pipeline stages: Trivy fs scan, build and push by digest, Trivy image scan, Syft SPDX SBOM, cosign sign and attest with azurekms://, cosign verify, deploy.
Kyverno ClusterPolicy that requires a valid signature for the protected ACR repository.
Local validating admission webhook that applies the same rule with real ECDSA signatures in Cosign's payload format.
Workload ID setup: user-assigned identity, federated credential, Key Vault RBAC and a SecretProviderClass.
projects.result: Unsigned test image: rejected. Signed image: admitted. Tag-only reference and a signature copied to another digest: rejected. Images outside the protected repository: unaffected.

demo.intro: Only images signed with the Key Vault key may run. A harmless unsigned image is turned away at admission.
captions: An ECDSA P-256 signing key is created. In the pipeline this key lives in Azure Key Vault.
Two harmless synthetic images are built and identified by digest.
Only the release image is signed, and the signature verifies.
Admission decisions: the unsigned, tag-only and tampered images are rejected; the signed image is admitted.

projects.home_problem: Any pullable image could run on AKS, and nobody knew what was inside it.
projects.home_result: Unsigned, tag-only and tampered images were rejected at admission; the signed image was admitted.
projects.environment: Azure Pipelines with Trivy, Syft (SPDX SBOM) and Cosign using an Azure Key Vault key; Kyverno verifyImages on AKS; Entra Workload ID and the Secrets Store CSI driver for secrets.
scope: Real ECDSA P-256 signing in Cosign's payload format and a local admission webhook, 9 tests
Trivy, Syft, Cosign, Kyverno on AKS and Workload ID
decisions: Push and deploy by digest, and have Kyverno verify the digest (mutateDigest and verifyDigest), so a tag cannot be swapped after signing.
Keep the signing key in Key Vault (azurekms://) so the pipeline never holds the private key.
Enforce in the admission policy, not just in the pipeline, so images from any source are checked.
Use Workload ID instead of stored credentials to read Key Vault secrets.
projects.failure: A harmless unsigned image, a tag-only reference, and a signature copied onto a different digest are submitted to the cluster.
projects.recovery: All three are rejected at admission. The image signed with the Key Vault key is admitted; images outside the protected repository are unaffected.
projects.evidence_gaps: The local webhook applies the same rule as the Kyverno policy; the Kyverno policy itself has not been run on an AKS cluster here.
projects.home_built: Trivy scans, an SBOM and Cosign signing with a Key Vault key, enforced at admission.

projects.title: Azure Functions Event-Driven Processing
projects.short: Queue-triggered function with idempotency, retries, poison-message handling and structured logs.
projects.problem: Queue redelivery charged customers twice, and malformed events kept retrying until they were dropped.
built: Idempotency key claimed before the side effect and completed after it; atomic on Table Storage.
Transient errors retried through the queue; permanent errors sent straight to the poison queue.
Structured JSON logs and a local runtime that reproduces queue delivery semantics.
projects.result: ORD-1 was delivered three times and recorded once. A transient failure succeeded on the third try; a malformed message and a message that failed five times went to the poison queue.

demo.intro: The same order arrives three times and is processed once.
captions: Duplicate delivery and a lost acknowledgement: two of three deliveries are recognised as duplicates.
Two transient 503 errors are retried; the third attempt succeeds.
A malformed message goes straight to the poison queue.
A message that fails on every attempt is moved to poison after five dequeues.
The ledger holds exactly one entry per order.

projects.home_problem: Queue redelivery charged customers twice, and malformed events retried until dropped.
projects.home_result: ORD-1 was delivered three times and recorded once; bad messages went to the poison queue.
projects.environment: An Azure Functions (Python v2) queue trigger with Storage Queues, Table Storage for idempotency and Application Insights; a local runtime reproduces queue delivery, visibility timeouts and maxDequeueCount 5.
scope: Processor and local queue runtime, 19 tests (in-memory and SQLite stores)
Function App, storage account and Application Insights
decisions: Claim an idempotency key before the side effect and complete it after, atomically in Table Storage.
Classify errors: transient errors are retried through the queue, permanent ones go straight to poison.
Structured JSON logs with the order ID and attempt number on every line.
projects.failure: The same order is delivered three times after a lost acknowledgement; the ledger returns HTTP 503 twice; one message is malformed and one fails on every attempt.
projects.recovery: Duplicates are recognised and skipped, the transient failure succeeds on the third attempt, the malformed message goes straight to poison, and the always-failing message moves to poison after five dequeues.
projects.evidence_gaps: The queue behaviour comes from the local runtime; it has not been run on a Function App.
projects.home_built: A queue-triggered Function with idempotency, retry classification and poison handling.

projects.title: Azure Disaster Recovery and Restore Drill
projects.short: Repeatable backup and restore drill with checksum verification and measured RTO and RPO.
projects.problem: Backups existed but had never been restored, RTO and RPO were never measured, and there was no proof a restore was complete.
built: Synthetic dataset, read-only snapshots with SHA-256 manifests, restore and verification.
Drill that deletes the data on purpose and writes a report with RTO and RPO against targets.
Azure script using Blob point-in-time restore, plus a runbook.
projects.result: 1,000 of 1,037 records restored with all checksums matching; the 37 records written after the backup are the measured RPO loss. RTO 7 minutes against a 30-minute target, RPO 45 minutes against 60.

demo.intro: Data is deleted on purpose, restored, and proven complete.
captions: A synthetic dataset is backed up; 37 more orders arrive after the backup.
The primary dataset is deleted and the integrity check fails.
The latest backup is restored and every file checksum matches the manifest.
RTO and RPO are measured against their targets and a drill report is written.

projects.home_problem: Backups existed but had never been restored, and RTO and RPO were never measured.
projects.home_result: 1,000 of 1,037 records restored with matching checksums; RTO 7 min (target 30), RPO 45 min (target 60).
projects.environment: A synthetic orders archive with read-only snapshots and SHA-256 manifests locally; an Azure script for Blob point-in-time restore with versioning, change feed and soft delete.
decisions: Prove a restore with per-file SHA-256 checksums and record counts, not just a successful copy.
Make snapshots read-only as a stand-in for immutable backups.
Delete the data on purpose during the drill and measure RTO and RPO against targets in a written report.
projects.failure: The primary dataset is deleted and the integrity check fails. 37 orders were written after the last backup.
projects.recovery: The latest backup is restored and every checksum matches the manifest. The 37 later records are the measured RPO loss.
projects.evidence_gaps: Measured in the local drill; the Azure point-in-time restore script has not been run here.
projects.home_built: A backup-and-restore drill with checksum verification and measured RTO and RPO.
